summary: Discusses a name-based Service Function Forwarder for service function chaining, separating the logical service path from the choice of where each function runs. This could make it faster to switch among execution locations in cloud or fog setups than rechaining with IP endpoints.

plainLanguage.summary: If a helper moves to another room, you should call them by name, not by room number. This lets traffic follow a service by name when it moves.

subtitle: Simplify service routing by using names instead of addresses.

tldr.problem: Service Function Chaining requires services to be identified by IP or MAC addresses, so when a virtualized service moves to a different location, the entire chain must be reconfigured with new address information, creating overhead in orchestration.
tldr.mechanism: Services are identified by names (e.g., URIs like www.example.com/service) instead of addresses. A name-based Service Function Forwarder (nSFF) resolves names to current execution locations using a Name Resolver, keeping the logical service path unchanged when services move.
tldr.outcome: Service operators can move service instances between data centers or cloud instances without reconfiguring the service chain. The logical path remains stable while the Name Resolver handles dynamic endpoint discovery.

facts.label: Service identification
facts.value: By name (URI) rather than IP/MAC address

today: RFC 8677 is an Informational document, an independent submission not representing IETF consensus. It presents InterDigital's approach to name-based service chaining for edge data centers and 5G networks. Implementation in production networks is limited; the approach remains a design proposal for future standardization.

sections.title: The Challenge of Dynamic Service Deployment
sections.content:
Service Function Chaining (SFC), defined in RFC 7665, chains network services together by routing packets through them in sequence. Traditional SFC identifies each service by its IP address or MAC address, and the Service Function Forwarder (SFF) forwards packets based on these Layer 2 or Layer 3 addresses.

With modern cloud and edge computing, services are increasingly virtualized and can be instantiated in different data centers or even different locations on demand. When a service instance moves, its IP address changes, which means the service chain must be reconfigured with the new addresses. In highly dynamic environments—such as 5G networks with distributed control planes—this reconfiguration creates significant orchestration overhead.

This RFC proposes lifting the SFC chain definition to the level of service names rather than addresses. Services are identified by names (such as URIs), and a Name Resolver maps those names to current execution locations, allowing the chain definition to remain unchanged even as services move.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a delivery chain where packages go through an inspection station, a payment counter, and a shipping depot. If the inspection station moves to a different building, do you redraw the entire chain, or do you just look up 'Inspection Station' to find its new location? Name-based routing does the latter.

sections.title: The Name-Based Service Function Path
sections.content:
Instead of a service chain like 192.0.2.1 → 198.51.100.10 → 198.51.100.15, a name-based service path (nSFP) looks like 192.0.x.x → www.example.com/smf → www.example.com/amf → www.example2.com/service1. Services are identified by URIs or other names that persist even when the underlying execution location changes.

The key insight is that a logical service path can map to multiple replicated instances of each service. If a single service (e.g., 'amf' in a 5G control plane) is deployed in three data centers, the name stays the same but the Name Resolver points traffic to different endpoints based on load, proximity, or availability.

The nSFF extends the SFF to understand name-based routing. When a packet arrives at an nSFF carrying Service Function Path (SFP) information, the nSFF looks up the current name-to-address mapping and forwards the packet accordingly. Subsequent packets over the same SFP may be forwarded to different instances if the mapping changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The service chain is written in names: 'Step 1: Payment, Step 2: Verification, Step 3: Shipping.' Each time a packet goes through, the current location of each service is looked up and used. If Verification moved from Building A to Building B, packets automatically start going to Building B without changing the chain.

sections.title: Components and Operation
sections.content:
The nSFF extends the traditional SFF and maintains a name-based Network Locator Map (nNLM) that associates Service Path Index (SPI), Service Index (SI), and service names with transport encapsulation information. For example, an nNLM entry maps (SPI=10, SI=253) to 'www.example.com' and specifies HTTP as the transport.

A new component called the Name Resolver (NR) resolves service names to current execution endpoints. When an nSFF needs to forward traffic to a remote service whose location is not in its local cache, it queries the NR. The NR responds with routing information (a pathID) that allows the packet to reach the service's current location. The nSFF caches this mapping for future packets.

The RFC illustrates operation using HTTP as the transport protocol. Packets flowing through the chain carry the NSH (Network Service Header) from RFC 8300, which identifies the SFP and current service index. The nSFF reads the NSH, looks up the next service name in the nNLM, resolves the name to an address (either locally cached or via the NR), and forwards the packet. Local services are reached via TCP connections; remote services are reached by encapsulating the packet with forwarding information and sending it through the network to the next nSFF.
sections.plainLanguage: The nSFF keeps a map of (service path, position) to service name and how to reach it. It also keeps a cache of name-to-address lookups. When a packet arrives, the nSFF reads what step it is at, looks up the service name, checks the cache or asks the Name Resolver where it is now, and sends it there.

sections.title: How Packets Flow Through the Network
sections.content:
When a packet enters an nSFF carrying NSH information with a specific SPI and SI, the nSFF:

1. Removes any existing transport encapsulation (TE).

2. Reads the NSH to determine the current service index and looks up the corresponding service name in its nNLM.

3. If the service is registered locally at this nSFF, it forwards the packet directly to the local service instance via TCP (for HTTP-based transactions).

4. If the service is remote, the nSFF checks its local cache for a pathID (forwarding path) associated with that service name. If found, it uses it; otherwise, it queries the Name Resolver.

5. The NR responds with a pathID that encodes routing information (typically derived from IPv6 addresses) pointing to the next nSFF that can reach the service.

6. The nSFF encapsulates the packet with the pathID and sends it via the network (using SDN switches or other forwarding mechanisms) to reach the remote nSFF.

7. The remote nSFF removes the encapsulation, reads the NSH again, and repeats the process for the next service in the path.

When a service sends a response back (such as an HTTP response), the nSFF maintains mappings of the original request's socket and pathID, so the response can be returned to the originating service.
sections.plainLanguage: When a packet arrives at nSFF1 for service 'payment-processor': (1) it checks the local cache for where 'payment-processor' is right now; (2) if found, it sends the packet there; (3) if not found, it asks the Name Resolver; (4) the resolver says 'it is over at nSFF2's location'; (5) nSFF1 packages the packet and sends it to nSFF2; (6) nSFF2 looks up where the actual service instance is and delivers the packet. Responses come back the same way.

sections.title: Advantages and Use Cases
sections.content:
This approach is particularly valuable in edge computing and 5G control planes. In a 5G network, control-plane functions (like the Session Management Function and Access and Mobility Management Function) are increasingly deployed as microservices across distributed data centers. With name-based SFC, operators can relocate a service instance in response to user mobility or changing load without updating the orchestration model; the name stays the same, and the Name Resolver points to the new location.

The method also simplifies configuration. Instead of updating next-hop information across multiple SFFs when a service moves, operators only need to update the Name Resolver. Subsequent traffic automatically uses the new location. The orchestrator can prepopulate name-to-address mappings at deployment time to avoid lookup latency on first use.

The design maintains backward compatibility: nSFFs can still work with traditional IP-addressed service functions if the nNLM contains IP addresses instead of names.
sections.plainLanguage: In a 5G network, when your phone connects, its session goes through multiple services spread across different data centers. With this approach, if a service needs to move closer to you (to reduce latency) or to a less-loaded data center, the chain definition does not change; the system just looks up the new location and routes to it.
